1.definition: An early Neolithic farming culture on the shores of Lake Faiyum in Egypt, roughly 5500–4000 BCE — one of the oldest agricultural communities in the Nile valley, known for grain-storage pits, sickle blades, and simple pottery.

A late-Predynastic Egyptian royal tomb at Abydos (ca. 3250 BCE) containing some of the earliest known Egyptian writing — small bone and ivory labels with proto-hieroglyphic signs, among the oldest writing anywhere in the world.

2.definition: A French archaeologist who led the research team that, in 2020, produced the first probable partial decipherment of Linear Elamite — a script that had stumped scholars for over a century.

4.matchText: witnesses and seals and formal contracts

5.definition: A bronze-casting method where the clay mold is built from several interlocking sections that fit together before the metal is poured, then taken apart afterward — letting craftsmen cast huge, intricate vessels.

A monumental U-shaped temple complex on the central Peruvian coast near modern Lima, built and used roughly 1500–800 BCE — part of the independent Andean tradition of large ceremonial architecture that rose at the same time as Elam's ziggurat-building peak.

A U-shaped ceremonial center in the Lurín valley south of modern Lima, Peru, dating to roughly 1500–1000 BCE — one of several monumental coastal temple sites the Andean peoples raised independently during Elam's Middle Elamite era.

A large adobe ceremonial complex in the Moche valley of north-coastal Peru, built in the second millennium BCE and famous for its monumental clay friezes — a flagship of the Andean monument-building tradition that paralleled Elam's at the opposite end of the world.

The highland Elamite king (reigned c. 1400 BCE) who founded the Igihalkid dynasty and began rebuilding Elam's external power after a century of diminished visibility; his line produced Untash-Napirisha, the builder of Chogha Zanbil.

The era of Elamite history running roughly 1500–1100 BCE, after the Sukkalmah and before the long Neo-Elamite decline — the kingdom's aggressive building-boom peak, when it joined the great powers of the Late Bronze Age Near East and raised monuments like Chogha Zanbil.

6.definition: An Elamite king, son of Shutruk-Nahhunte (the king who sacked Babylon), who carried on his father's wars against Babylon before the throne passed to his brother Shilhak-Inshushinak.

A famous Elamite bronze sculpture, made under King Shilhak-Inshushinak, showing two figures in a ritual scene; its name means roughly "sunrise," and it's one of the great surviving works of Elamite metalwork.

A four-sided diorite pillar carved in the 23rd century BCE recording land purchases made during the reign of the Akkadian king Manishtushu. Looted from Mesopotamia to Susa by Shutruk-Nahhunte and excavated there by French archaeologists, it is now in the Louvre.

The roughly 350-year stretch (about 1100 to 750 BCE) after the fall of Middle Elamite power, during which Elam nearly vanishes from the written record — occupation continued at Susa and Anshan, but the monumental building and trophy-collecting of the imperial age stopped, and outside chronicles mention Elam only in passing.

7.definition: A set of carved alabaster panels from Ashurbanipal's palace at Nineveh, also called the Banquet Scene, showing the Assyrian king and his queen reclining on couches in a garden, drinking wine and being fanned by servants, while the severed head of the defeated Elamite king Te-Umman hangs from a nearby tree. Carved around 645 BCE and now in the British Museum, it is one of the most famous and chilling images to survive from the ancient Near East.

8.definition: The final phase of independent Elam (roughly 1100–540 BCE): after the collapse of the great Middle Elamite empire, Elam fragmented into smaller highland kingdoms and city-states that revived briefly, clashed repeatedly with Assyria, and were finally crushed when Ashurbanipal sacked Susa in the 640s BCE.
